title: Host swap surge & memory-accounting discrepancy - postmortem
content:
Summary:
On 2026-02-25 10:03 UTC we observed a cluster-wide latency spike that correlated with a subset of serving hosts entering swap. The spike caused tail latency regressions for the hosted-api surface (95p -> 1.8s, 99p -> 3.6s) and triggered automated failovers for 6 nodes. No user data was lost and the platform remained available, but customer-facing SLOs were breached for ~28 minutes.

Impact:
- Duration: ~28 minutes of elevated tail latency and 6 node failovers.
- Services affected: hosted inference endpoints (text generation), internal e2e tests, some Dedicated tenants using the same host pool.
- Customer impact: increased response times, a small number of requests retried by clients. No model correctness issues reported.

What happened (brief):
A change in continuous-batching memory accounting in the serving runtime (PR referenced below) caused transient per-request memory to be undercounted during prefetch and KV cache operations when requests had large prompt prefixes. Under high QPS, the undercount allowed the node to accept more concurrent microbatches than its true physical memory could support. When background GC-like processes (runtime cache compaction + periodic model-side prefetch) ran concurrently, host RSS exceeded physical memory and the kernel began swapping. Swapping dramatically increased scheduling latency for the inference threads and blocked batching progress, causing both tail latency spikes and a cascade where the autoscaler marked nodes as unhealthy, triggering failovers.

Timeline (UTC):
- 09:58 - Canary dashboards show small latency uptick on one region.
- 10:03 - Pager alerts for 99p latency and elevated swap pressure on hosts pool-a.
- 10:04 - SRE on-call joins Slack channel and starts collecting logs.
- 10:07 - 3 hosts report >1GB swap used. Autoscaler marks two nodes unhealthy and removes them from the pool.
- 10:12 - Engineering suspects recent memory-accounting change in serving-runtime PR #1984.
- 10:20 - Mitigation: temporarily reduce batching window and reject requests exceeding a per-request memory heuristic.
- 10:30 - Swap usage declines as prefetch backlog drains; latency returns to baseline.
- 10:45 - Full rollback planned and queued for low-traffic window; follow-up testing scheduled.

Root cause analysis:
Primary root cause: a regression in the continuous-batching memory accounting logic that omitted transient prefetch allocations from the per-request accounting bucket when a request used both prefetch and KV-cache reads. This allowed an optimistic concurrency limit that didn't reflect actual RSS.
Contributing factors:
- Prefetch/compaction tasks run on the same CPU/memory cgroups and are not accounted to per-request budgets.
- Host kernel swap enabled for the instance type; swap usage magnified tail latency instead of OOM-killing (which would have been surfaced differently).
- Autoscaler health checks are sensitive to response latency but do not inspect swap or memory accounting metrics when making immediate failover decisions, leading to cascade.
- The memory-accounting change was rolled out to the pool without staggered ramp (canary size too small for this failure mode).

Why did swap happen rather than OOM kill?
Swap was enabled on the instance image to provide temporary breathing room during maintenance tasks. Because the kernel did not detect an immediate OOM (allocations were satisfied via swap), processes remained alive but extremely slow. This made the incident a tail-latency problem rather than immediate crashes.

Detection and diagnostics performed:
- Correlated host vmstat /proc/meminfo with application-level memory accounting logs and batching concurrency metrics.
- Verified commit window for serving-runtime PR #1984 and replayed the accounting logic locally with synthetic workload.
- Grepped audit logs to show simultaneous increase in prefetch throughput and KV cache compaction events at incident start.
- Heap and native allocator sampling on affected nodes confirmed additional ~12–18% RSS per request in certain request shapes (long prompt + embeddings cache miss).

Immediate mitigations applied (chronological):
1) Reduced batching window from 40ms to 25ms for pool-a to lower concurrency headroom (10:20).
2) Enabled conservative per-request memory rejection heuristic (hard reject requests estimated >X MB) to reduce peak concurrent working set (10:22).
3) Temporarily disabled prefetch compaction background job on the affected hosts (10:24).
4) Rebalanced traffic away from pool-a into warm spare pool-b while we validated mitigations (10:28).
Effect: swap pressure subsided and tail latency returned to baseline by ~10:30.

Longer-term fixes and action items (owners and due dates):
- eng-serving-runtime: revert the accounting change and add unit tests to cover prefetch+kv codepath (owner: Sara Chen, due: 2026-03-04).
- eng-serving-runtime: implement end-to-end e2e workload test that simulates large prompt prefixes under high QPS and prefetch activity (owner: Ethan Brooks, due: 2026-03-15).
- eng-sre: add host swap/generic swap-in-progress metric to autoscaler decision signals and alerting (owner: Miguel Alvarez, due: 2026-03-08).
- infra: create an image variant with swap disabled for serving pools that must meet strict tail latency SLOs and roll it out as optional pool config (owner: Rina Sato, due: 2026-04-01).
- platform-engineering: modify deployment runbook to require staged ramp (canary >= 10% traffic for 1hr) for memory-accounting or batching changes (owner: Asha Patel, due: 2026-03-05).
- Observability/product: add synthetic canary tests that include cache miss and long-prefix prompts (owner: Product-hosted-api, due: 2026-03-12).

Runbook updates (to be merged):
- New checklist for "swap pressure" incident type: include quick checks for /proc/meminfo, vmstat si/so, and per-host accounting mismatch.
- Add a mitigation recipe: disable background compaction/prefetch, reduce batching window, enable per-request hardness budget, and shift traffic.
- Autoscaler tuning guideline: do not evict nodes solely on tail latency unless swap > threshold or mem accounting mismatch confirmed.

Testing and validation plan for fixes:
- Unit + integration tests on accounting logic that cover combined prefetch + kv-cache paths.
- Local stress tests with artifact that produces long-prefix prompts and forced cache misses while ramping QPS to target concurrency profiles.
- Deploy accounting revert to a small canary (2 hosts) for 24 hours with synthetic canaries exercising the prefetch path.
- Run chaos test that toggles swap on/off to ensure behavior matches expected mitigation recipes.

Post-incident learnings and notes:
- Memory accounting correctness for composite request flows is critical; isolated unit tests missed the combined path.
- Swap can hide immediate OOMs but creates much worse tail latency problems for serving workloads; our default images should lean toward swap-off for inference-critical pools.
- Autoscaler decisions that only use latency are brittle; adding system-level signals (swap, mem_used_pct, per-request-accounting-gap) improves stability.
- Canary sizing and ramp rules must be explicit for changes that affect resource accounting.

Appendix (investigation artifacts):
- Relevant PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pulls/1984
- Jira ticket: JIRA-SRE-4721
- Slack timeline: slack:#sre-oncall:msg-abc123
- Heap/native allocator samples attached to ticket (link in Jira).

Open questions for follow-up meeting:
- Should we make swap-off the default for all serving images and add an ops toggle for rare maintenance use?
- Are there other composite accounting paths (e.g., streaming + function-calling) that our tests don't exercise?
- What guardrails should we add to PR reviews for runtime accounting changes?

Conclusion:
This incident was caused by a missed accounting path in the serving runtime that allowed the host working set to silently exceed physical memory under a realistic workload shape. The immediate mitigations were effective and prevented customer-facing outages. The recommended long-term changes (revert + tests, autoscaler signals, image changes, and runbook additions) will reduce the risk of recurrence.

Prepared by: Asha Patel (SRE)
Reviewed by: Miguel Alvarez, Sara Chen
